track.label: Personal Branding & LinkedIn
track.summary: Build a professional presence that opens doors — from clarifying your personal brand and optimising your LinkedIn profile to creating content consistently, growing your network, and establishing thought leadership in your field.
track.name: personal-branding

phases.title: Personal Brand Foundations
phases.description: Clarify what your personal brand actually is, who it's for, what makes it distinctive, and why it matters for your career — before you write a single post.

phases.title: LinkedIn Profile Optimisation
phases.description: Transform your LinkedIn profile from a digital CV into a magnet for opportunities — with a standout headline, keyword-rich About section, and featured content that shows your work.

phases.title: Content Strategy & Writing
phases.description: Develop a content strategy that's sustainable and authentic — choosing your format, building a posting rhythm, and writing hooks and posts that people actually read.

phases.title: Network Building
phases.description: Grow your network with intention — reaching out to the right people, engaging meaningfully rather than broadcasting, and building real professional relationships.

phases.title: Thought Leadership
phases.description: Move from posting to leading — writing long-form articles, starting a LinkedIn newsletter, and establishing expertise that gets you invited into rooms and opportunities.

phases.title: Personal Website & Portfolio
phases.description: Build the digital home for your career — a personal website with your portfolio, case studies, and a unified online presence across platforms.

topics.title: What Is a Personal Brand and Why It Matters
topics.description: Understand personal branding as the intersection of your expertise, your values, and the problems you solve — and why professionals with strong brands get better opportunities.

steps.d: Write down what you're known for at work, what you actually want to be known for, and what gap exists between those two.
List three specific skills or domains where you have unusual depth or accomplishment—these are your brand foundation.
Describe the person most likely to hire you, partner with you, or refer you—their role, industry, and the problem you solve for them.
Write one sentence that captures your perspective or value that's different from other people in your field.
Share your brand definition with two people who know your work and ask if that's how they see you.

topics.title: Identifying Your Niche and Value Proposition
topics.description: Define the specific audience your brand serves, the unique angle you bring, and the value you create — so you stop trying to appeal to everyone and start resonating with someone.

steps.d: Narrow from your entire field to the specific people you want to reach: title, industry, problem they have, or goal they're pursuing.
Write down the specific problem your audience has that you uniquely solve—not generic skill, but the concrete thing they struggle with.
Identify three things about you or your approach that someone else in your field doesn't offer: experience, perspective, background, or results.
Write a one-sentence statement combining your expertise, your audience, and the specific problem you solve: "I help [audience] [achieve what] by [unique approach]."
Share your niche and value proposition with three people in your target audience and ask if it resonates with them.

topics.title: Auditing and Aligning Your Brand
topics.description: Audit your existing online presence — Google results, LinkedIn, social profiles — and identify the gaps between how you appear and how you want to be perceived.

steps.d: Google your name, check your LinkedIn, Twitter, and any other public profiles to see how you currently appear.
Note where your online presence doesn't match your brand—old job titles, outdated photos, inconsistent descriptions, or negative results.
Read your LinkedIn headline, about section, and recent activity and score each for how well they communicate your brand (1-10).
Review your Twitter/X, GitHub, or other professional profiles and note whether the content aligns with your intended brand.
Summarize your online audit: what's working, what needs to change, and prioritize your top three fixes.

topics.title: LinkedIn Headline and About Section
topics.description: Write a LinkedIn headline that captures attention and communicates your value in one line, and an About section that tells your story and ends with a clear call to action.

steps.d: Write three different LinkedIn headlines (120 characters max) that each communicate your value from a different angle.
Select the headline that best captures your brand and includes keywords someone searching for people like you would use.
Compose a 200-300 word About section that tells your story, explains your expertise, and ends with a clear call to action (newsletter, contact, message).
Share your headline and About with a peer and ask if it's immediately clear what you do and why they should connect with you.
Publish your new headline and About section on LinkedIn and monitor connection requests for the next week to see if quality improved.

topics.title: Experience, Skills, and Featured Content
topics.description: Optimise your Experience section with achievement-oriented bullets, curate your Skills endorsements, and use the Featured section to showcase your best work front and centre.

steps.d: For your current or most recent role, replace generic duties with achievement-oriented bullets: quantify impact where possible and emphasize results.
Edit your LinkedIn skills section to include 8-10 skills that directly support your brand and remove outdated ones.
Add 3-5 links, documents, or images to your Featured section showcasing your best work, publications, or projects.
If your profile photo is more than two years old or doesn't match your intended brand, update it with a recent, professional headshot.
Check your LinkedIn completion score (shoot for 90%+) by adding missing fields: recommendations, volunteer work, or certifications.

topics.title: LinkedIn Algorithm and Profile SEO
topics.description: Understand how the LinkedIn search algorithm ranks profiles, which keywords to embed, and how profile completeness and engagement signals affect your visibility.

steps.d: Identify which profile fields are weighted most by LinkedIn search: headline, skills, recommendations, and recent activity.
Add 5-7 keywords to your headline, about, and experience that people searching your expertise would use.
Post or engage with content twice a week for two weeks and observe whether your profile is appearing higher in searches.
Request three skill endorsements and one written recommendation from peers—profiles with recent recommendations rank higher.
Ask a peer to search LinkedIn for keywords matching your brand and note what position you appear in their results.

topics.title: LinkedIn Post Formats That Perform
topics.description: Learn which post formats drive the most reach and engagement — single-image posts, carousels, text-only posts, and polls — and when to use each one.

steps.d: Review five LinkedIn posts from creators in your field that got high engagement and note the format: text-only, carousel, single image, poll, or video.
Based on the formats you saw, test three different formats in your first three posts and track which gets the most profile visits.
Take one insight from your work or experience and create three versions: a text post, a carousel, and an image post.
Post all three versions over two weeks and track engagement rates—note which format your audience prefers.
Choose the format you'll use most often and aim to post 50% of your content in that format going forward.

topics.title: Building a Content Calendar and Routine
topics.description: Create a sustainable content calendar — batching content, planning content pillars, choosing a realistic posting frequency, and building a system that keeps you consistent.

steps.d: Identify three topics you'd like to be known for (e.g., career growth, industry trends, team building) that align with your brand.
Design a weekly rotation: two posts on pillar one, one on pillar two, one on pillar three—consistency over perfection.
Write and schedule 4-8 posts for the month in one sitting, spacing them across days so you publish consistently without daily writing.
Commit to a realistic posting cadence: 2x weekly, weekly, or 2x monthly—consistency matters more than volume.
Follow your content calendar for four weeks and check whether regular posting improved your profile views or connection requests.

topics.title: Writing Hooks and Compelling Opening Lines
topics.description: Master the first line of every post — the hook that stops the scroll — using proven patterns like bold statements, stories, statistics, and provocative questions.

steps.d: Find five LinkedIn posts with high comments/reactions and mark exactly what the first sentence does: bold claim, surprising stat, story setup, or provocative question.
Create three template hooks for yourself: one for bold claims, one for curiosity, one for relatability—use these for your upcoming posts.
Write opening lines for ten posts using your hook patterns, ensuring the first sentence will stop someone scrolling.
Post these ten hooks over the next month and track which opening styles get the most initial engagement (likes/comments in first hour).
Based on performance, identify which hook pattern works best for your audience and use it in 60% of your future posts.

topics.title: Working Out Who to Reach
topics.description: The step before outreach: building a named list of the right people and knowing one real thing about each.

steps.t: Define the role, not the person
steps.d: Write the job title, company type and seniority you need. "Analyst at a mid-market PE fund in Mumbai" is actionable; "someone in finance" is not.

steps.t: Build a list of twenty names
steps.d: Use LinkedIn search filters, alumni directories and company team pages. Twenty, in a spreadsheet, with their company and role.

steps.t: Find one specific thing about each
steps.d: A post they wrote, a deal they worked, a talk they gave. Without it your message is a template and reads like one.
A second-degree connection two years ahead of you replies far more often than a managing director. Start there.
For each name, write who could introduce you. A referred message gets answered at several times the rate of a cold one.

topics.title: Strategic Connection Requests and Outreach
topics.description: Reach out in a way that gets accepted — personalised messages, relevant context, and clear mutual value — rather than generic requests that go ignored.

steps.d: Write down 20 people you'd want in your network: potential collaborators, industry leaders, peers, and people one or two layers above your current role.
Write 10 customized connection requests to people on your list, referencing something specific about them or a reason you want to connect.
Send your first 10 personalized requests over two weeks, mentioning a mutual connection, a shared interest, or something you admire about them.
Note how many requests you send, who accepts, and whether the acceptance rate is higher than generic requests.
Review which requests got accepted and which didn't—note common factors in your most successful outreach.

topics.title: Engaging Authentically with Your Network
topics.description: Build presence through consistent engagement — thoughtful comments, meaningful reactions, and sharing others' work in ways that add your perspective.

steps.d: Find a post from someone in your network or target network and write a thoughtful comment that adds new insight rather than just agreeing.
For five days, write one substantive comment on someone else's post per day—not emojis, but something that adds value.
Repost three interesting posts or articles from your network with your own commentary about why it matters.

steps.t: Build a habit of reciprocal engagement
steps.d: When someone engages with your posts, engage back on one of theirs within a few days.
Track how much your comment activity increases profile visits and new connections over two weeks.

topics.title: DMs, Follow-Ups, and Relationship Building
topics.description: Turn connections into conversations — the anatomy of a good LinkedIn DM, when and how to follow up, and the long-game mindset that builds professional relationships.

steps.d: Write a DM to a new connection that references something they posted or something about them, adds value, and asks a genuine question.
Reach out to five new connections with personalized messages that aren't asking for anything—just building rapport.
When someone engages with your post, send them a DM within 48 hours acknowledging their comment and continuing the conversation.
For key connections, add reminders to re-engage every 4-8 weeks with a new message, article, or genuine check-in.
After one month of intentional DM engagement, identify which connections turned into real conversations or opportunities.

topics.title: LinkedIn Long-Form Articles and Newsletter
topics.description: Launch a LinkedIn newsletter or article series to build a subscriber base, demonstrate deep expertise, and give your audience a reason to come back week after week.

steps.d: Decide on a LinkedIn newsletter name, frequency (weekly or bi-weekly), and three core topics you'll consistently cover.
Publish your first edition with an introduction of what readers will get, and three pieces of substantive content or insight.
Promote your newsletter in your bio, mention it in posts, and ask your network to subscribe for the first month to build initial momentum.
Publish on your schedule for two months and track subscription growth and engagement rates.
Review which newsletter topics get the most engagement and double down on those themes.

topics.title: Building Credibility Through Expertise and Proof
topics.description: Establish the signals of credibility — case studies, testimonials, speaking engagements, certifications, and documented results that prove your expertise rather than just claiming it.

steps.d: Choose a project where you achieved a concrete outcome (revenue, time saved, process improved) and write down the before-and-after numbers.
Ask someone who benefited from your work to write a short testimonial about the specific impact you had—request they be specific with results.
Write or share a post about a successful project including: the problem, your approach, and the quantified result.
If you've earned relevant certifications or credentials, add them to your LinkedIn and feature them.
Volunteer to give a talk, host a webinar, or teach a class in your expertise area to establish authority.

topics.title: Collaborations, Guest Posts, and Media Features
topics.description: Amplify your reach through collaborations — co-creating content with other creators, pitching guest posts, getting quoted in industry publications, and finding podcast appearances.

steps.d: List three potential collaborators from adjacent fields, documenting one published piece each has created that demonstrates reach to your audience.
Reach out to one collaborator with a specific idea: co-write a post, do a recorded discussion, or guest post on each other's profiles.
Write a guest post for a publication or another creator's platform that introduces your expertise to their audience.
Find 10 podcasts or shows in your field that take guest experts and pitch yourself as a guest with a specific topic idea.
Get quoted in an article, interviewed on a show, or featured as an expert—use any media mention in your LinkedIn featured section.

topics.title: Building Your Personal Website
topics.description: Set up a personal website that serves as your home base — what pages to include, what platform to use, and the essential elements of a professional personal site.

steps.t: Choose a platform for your site
steps.d: Decide which platform works for you: WordPress, Webflow, Carrd, or a static site—choose based on your technical comfort and needs.
Register your name as a domain (.com preferred) so people can easily find you online.
Outline your site's pages: home (who you are and what you do), about (your story), work/portfolio, contact, and optional blog.
Create a basic five-page site with professional copy and photos—get it live rather than perfect.
Have three people unfamiliar with you visit your site and ask: What does she do? How would you contact her? Did you trust her?

topics.title: Portfolio Curation and Case Studies
topics.description: Build a portfolio that shows your best work — how to structure case studies, what to include, and how to present projects that demonstrate impact rather than just activity.

steps.d: Review your work and choose your three to five strongest projects or accomplishments to feature as case studies.
For one project, write: the challenge (what problem did you solve), your approach (what you did differently), and the result (quantified impact).

steps.t: Add visuals to your case study
steps.d: Include before-and-after screenshots, charts showing impact, or images of the work—visuals make case studies more compelling.
Follow the same structure for your other selected projects and build a portfolio demonstrating diverse skills and impact.
Create a portfolio or work page on your site linking to 3-5 case studies that visitors can click into.

topics.title: Integrating Your Full Online Presence
topics.description: Create a coherent cross-channel presence — linking your LinkedIn, personal site, newsletter, and other profiles so they reinforce each other and funnel the right people toward you.

steps.d: Review your LinkedIn, personal site, Twitter, newsletter, and any other profiles—note where descriptions, photos, or messaging conflict.
Use the same professional headshot across all platforms so you're instantly recognizable.
Write a version of your personal brand statement that works across platforms (LinkedIn, Twitter bio, website headline) with consistent phrasing.
Ensure every profile links to your personal website and your website links back to your major platforms: LinkedIn, Twitter, newsletter.
Start from your LinkedIn and follow the links to your site and vice versa—confirm the experience is cohesive and messaging consistent.
